summary: International education this week has three main threads. First, study-abroad policy continues to diverge: the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) proposes to charge universities $70,000 for each first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one; during the comment period the Presidents' Alliance and the University of Michigan formally submitted objections on 9–10 November. At the same time, Studyportals data show that page views of US on-campus programmes by international students rose 40% in 1–8 November, after the midterm elections. At the Australian International Education Conference (AIEC), Canada is shifting toward research graduate students (6,455 new graduate study permits in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the same period a year earlier), New Zealand is pursuing growth, and Australia is considering stricter financial-evidence rules. Second, Switzerland is pushing on both AI education and AI × scientific computing: EPFL announced on 12 November an undergraduate AI degree from the 2027–28 academic year; the same day ETH Zurich and EPFL together received three large ERC Synergy awards, focused on AI-accelerated supercomputing and mixed-precision algorithms (including quantum-chemistry simulation). Third, quantum talent training is moving down to the technician and undergraduate level: UCSB received about $994,000 to build hands-on courses for quantum technicians, and FAU received $3 million from the US Department of Labor for a talent pathway in quantum sensing and communications. In China, the International University Alliance for the Development of Digital and Intelligent Education, initiated by Peking University, signed with Lingnan University during the 2026 Beijing Forum, and the fourth general assembly of the China–Belarus University Alliance was held in Shanghai on 11 November. In philanthropy, the University of New Mexico received a bequest valued at $55 million (the largest in its history), and George Mason University received $30 million to establish two policy institutes.
trends: Study-abroad flows are highly policy-sensitive: the US OPT-fee proposal and the election result almost simultaneously changed student expectations; Canada, Australia and New Zealand are each adjusting, and the trend of students comparing multiple destinations is becoming clearer.

AI is moving from a tool to a standalone discipline: EPFL is creating an undergraduate AI degree with ethics and policy as required courses, and Chinese universities are advancing "digital and intelligent education" through alliances. Competition in AI education has extended to undergraduate foundations and to governance.

AI × high-performance computing × scientific simulation has become a focus of Europe's top research funding. ETH, EPFL, PSI and CSCS in Switzerland form a clear cluster, and directions such as quantum chemistry sit at the frontier where classical and quantum computing meet.

Quantum talent training is moving toward a full chain: from research doctorates out to technicians, community colleges and undergraduates, with industry micro-credentials and industrial equipment, emphasising hands-on skills.
University fundraising continues to rely on large and planned-bequest gifts, and tends to use gifts to establish themed institutes and scholarship funds.
footer: All facts and figures in this brief are taken from the public sources listed; the original texts prevail. Time window: 2026-11-06 to 2026-11-13 (Zurich time). This edition has no peer-reviewed education papers, newly released QS/THE/OECD/UNESCO annual reports this week, or Nature/Science-level results, and no permanent record was created.

items.title: DHS proposes high fees of $70,000 / $30,000 for OPT recommendations, and universities object collectively; international-student interest in the US rebounds 40% after the midterms
items.what: DHS issued a proposed rule on 8 October requiring universities to pay $70,000 when recommending an F-1 student for a first OPT (post-completion practical training) application, and $30,000 for each later recommendation (including a STEM OPT extension), on the grounds of combating fraud and preventing OPT from being used to bypass the H-1B. The Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration submitted public comments on 9 November and issued a statement on 10 November calling for the rule to be withdrawn in full, saying it would "effectively end the OPT programme". The University of Michigan published its objection the same day, questioning whether DHS had shown that the fee was necessary. According to Inside Higher Ed on 10 November, internal Studyportals data showed that after Democrats won control of Congress in the 3 November midterms, page views of US on-campus programmes rose 40% in 1–8 November. Earlier DHS data had shown that average international-student enrolment in 2025–26 was down 13%.
items.why: OPT is one of the core returns for international students choosing the United States. If the high fee takes effect, it will directly change the global cost-benefit structure of study abroad, and students may divert to Europe, Asia and elsewhere. The rapid rebound in interest after the election shows how sensitive students are to policy signals. The proposed rule is not yet in effect, and its final path is worth continued tracking.
items.src: Presidents' Alliance; University of Michigan International Center; Inside Higher Ed

items.title: AIEC global dialogue: Canada turns toward research graduate students, New Zealand pursues growth, Australia considers stricter financial evidence
items.what: According to Education Post on 10 November, in a global dialogue at the Australian International Education Conference (AIEC 2026, 27–30 October, Sydney): a head of the Canadian Bureau for International Education (CBIE) said Canada's international-student numbers had fallen from more than 1 million at the end of 2023 to under 700,000 at the end of 2025, but that 6,455 new graduate study permits were issued in the second quarter of 2026, more than double the 3,085 in the same period of 2025, with graduates exempt from the provincial attestation-letter requirement. New Zealand expects about 99,000 international students in 2026, and international-education export revenue is already above pre-pandemic levels. Australia's new overseas higher-education enrolments were down 4.9% year on year at the start of 2026 (The PIE News), and the Department of Home Affairs is consulting on "genuine student" assessment and financial evidence (including a proposal that funds be held in an Australian bank account); the 2027 planned cap on new enrolments remains 295,000.
items.why: The main English-speaking destinations are moving from "scale expansion" toward "structural choice": Canada clearly prefers research talent, Australia is tightening assessment, and New Zealand is treating international education as a growth tool. Global student mobility will depend more on policy stability and research opportunities.

items.title: EPFL announces an undergraduate degree in artificial intelligence from 2027–28, with AI ethics and policy as a required course
items.what: EPFL's School of Computer and Communication Sciences (IC) announced on 12 November that it would offer a bachelor's degree in artificial intelligence from the 2027–2028 academic year. The degree shares its first year (foundations in mathematics and computing) with the computer-science bachelor's, then splits from the second year; it will have tracks including AI theory, life sciences and robotics, and will work closely with the Institute of Mathematics. The degree includes a required course, "AI Ethics and Policy". First-year programming is taught in French, mathematics and physics may be taken in French or English, and the second and third years are taught entirely in English. Vice President for Education Nicolas Grandjean said the school is also developing an AI minor and interdisciplinary AI courses covering strategic directions such as sustainable development, the energy transition and medical innovation.
items.why: A leading Swiss technical university is raising AI from a branch of computer science to a standalone undergraduate discipline, and making ethics and policy required — a European path of AI education that emphasises foundations, interdisciplinarity and social responsibility. Teaching in English also raises its attractiveness to international students.

items.title: ERC Synergy awards land in Switzerland: ETH and EPFL/PSI lead projects on AI-accelerated supercomputing and mixed-precision algorithms
items.what: ETH Zurich announced on 12 November that two professors had received European Research Council (ERC) Synergy awards: computer-science professor Torsten Hoefler (also chief AI architect at the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre, CSCS) is taking part in a project with ETH, EPFL and the University of Manchester to use AI methods to speed key scientific applications by about 10 times and cut energy use by 3–5 times, with a total of €10 million, of which ETH receives €2.5 million; chemistry professor Ruth Signorell is leading a project on the chemistry of tiny water droplets (partners include France's CNRS, Germany's DESY and the University of Bristol), totalling €14 million, of which ETH receives €4.9 million. EPFL announced in the same period that mathematician Laura Grigori had received a Synergy award to lead the RaMPA project (with PSI as a partner), combining randomisation and mixed precision to provide faster, more energy-efficient computational methods for climate modelling, molecular simulation and quantum chemistry.
items.why: Europe's highest-tier collaborative research funding is flowing toward "AI × high-performance computing × scientific simulation". ETH, EPFL, PSI and CSCS in Switzerland form a clear national-level cluster, sitting at the frontier where quantum computing and classical supercomputing will meet.

items.title: Quantum talent training moves down the chain: UCSB receives about $994,000 for technician practical courses; FAU receives $3 million for a talent pathway in quantum sensing and communications
items.what: UC Santa Barbara announced on 6 November that it had received $993,909 from the California Workforce Development Board to launch the Q-COAST (optics, advanced vacuum and superconducting training alliance) project, building three hands-on courses with Central Coast community colleges, employment agencies and companies: operation of vacuum and cryogenic equipment, fabrication and testing of photonic integrated circuits, and quantum-optics experiments. The courses will connect to IEEE micro-credentials, with development starting in January 2027 and a summer 2028 pilot. Florida Atlantic University (FAU) announced on 10 November a $3 million five-year award (1 October 2026 to 30 September 2031) under the US Department of Labor's Strengthening Community Colleges initiative, working with Infleqtion to introduce Rydberg-atom quantum radio-frequency sensing and communications equipment and an optical atomic clock, and to build a training pathway in quantum sensing and communications from early undergraduate to graduate level, expected to cover more than 100 students. FAU is also preparing to install a D-Wave Advantage2 quantum computer.
items.why: Quantum education is expanding from the doctoral and research level to technicians, community colleges and undergraduates, and is tied directly to micro-credentials and industrial equipment, a sign that what industrialisation most lacks is engineering and technical talent who can "get the equipment running".
items.src: UC Santa Barbara College of Engineering; Florida Atlantic University News

items.tag: University alliances / digital and intelligent education
items.title: The Peking University-initiated International University Alliance for the Development of Digital and Intelligent Education signs with Lingnan University, planning an Asia-Pacific centre; the fourth general assembly of the China–Belarus University Alliance is held in Shanghai
items.what: According to a Lingnan University press release on 10 November, President Qin Sizhao attended the 2026 Beijing Forum and a special forum on digital and intelligent education on 6–7 November, and signed a memorandum of understanding on behalf of Lingnan with the International University Alliance for the Development of Digital and Intelligent Education (DI-IDEA), initiated by Peking University and bringing together more than 30 universities worldwide. The two sides will explore jointly building a "Lingnan–DI-IDEA Joint Centre and DI-IDEA Asia-Pacific Centre" (working title), and consider locating it in the university town of Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis, focused on industry–academia–research collaboration and the translation of educational science and technology results. A presidents' round table included the London School of Economics, the Hong Kong Polytechnic University and the University of Strathclyde. According to the Ministry of Education website, the fourth general assembly of the China–Belarus University Alliance was held in Shanghai on 11 November; Minister of Education Huai Jinpeng delivered a video address, and universities on both sides reached several cooperation agreements on talent training and joint research.
items.why: Chinese universities are advancing international cooperation in education in the AI era through "alliances + regional centres", and the university town in Hong Kong's Northern Metropolis is becoming a new landing point for cooperation between mainland and international universities.
items.src: Lingnan University press release; Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

items.title: The University of New Mexico receives a bequest valued at $55 million (the largest in its history); George Mason University receives $30 million to establish two policy institutes
items.what: The University of New Mexico (UNM) and its foundation announced on 11 November an anonymous planned-bequest gift valued at about $55 million, the largest philanthropic commitment in the university's history. Because the gift is a share of the future value of an estate, the final amount will depend on what is actually received. Funds will go to the College of Arts and Sciences, the College of Nursing, dental medicine, a graduate scholarship fund, the School of Medicine, a student emergency-aid fund and the Harwood Museum of Art, among others, as UNM advances a $1.2 billion comprehensive campaign. George Mason University announced on 9 November that Dwight Schar, founder of NVR, had given $30 million to establish, in the Schar School of Policy and Government, an Institute for Security, Intelligence and Defense and an Institute for Economic Statecraft (researching export controls, financial sanctions, tariffs and restrictions on critical technologies, among other topics), expected to start in autumn 2027.
items.why: Large gifts continue to concentrate on a mix of scholarships, research and new institutes, and planned bequests have become an important fundraising tool for US universities. The model of using a gift to establish a themed institute is worth watching.
items.src: UNM Newsroom; George Mason University News
